title: Accenture's $9 Billion Answer to the Question Nobody's Asking
subtitle: The world's largest IT-services firm doubled its acquisition budget to roughly $9 billion, snapped up two SAP specialists in a single week, and is betting the AI era still belongs to the people who install it.
summary: Accenture is answering the “AI eats consulting” question with a $9 billion acquisition spree — two SAP-focused mid-market deals this week, a doubled M&A budget, and a steady comeback from its June slide as analysts hike their targets.

bodyHtml:
What happens to the people who tell companies how to use AI, once the AI gets good enough to tell them itself? It's the question quietly haunting every consulting firm on the planet. And this week, Accenture — the biggest IT services firm on Earth — answered with a number: $9 billion.

Here's Accenture in plain English. It's the company the world's biggest businesses hire when they need to get modern fast — the firm that actually installs AI into the daily operations of the Fortune 500. You've seen its work even if you've never heard its name. Roughly 799,000 employees, about 9,000 clients, around $70 billion in revenue last fiscal year. If AI is the electricity, Accenture is the electrician — and the electrician just went shopping.

This week alone, it announced two acquisitions aimed squarely at the mid-market. COMWARE is a Tokyo-based SAP specialist with 180-plus professionals and a partnership with SAP Japan stretching back more than 25 years. McCoy is a Dutch SAP Gold Partner with 380-plus professionals spread across the Netherlands, Spain, and the Philippines. Terms weren't disclosed for either, but the message was loud: Accenture wants the companies that are too small for the Fortune 500 but too big to ignore.

Both bolt onto Accenture Edge, the mid-market business the firm launched back in June for companies pulling in between $300 million and $3 billion a year. Why should you care? Because that slice of the market — a roughly $240 billion opportunity growing high single digits — is where the next wave of enterprise AI spending happens. The biggest companies already have armies of consultants. The mid-market is wide open, and Accenture is planting its flag first.

This is the through-line of fiscal 2026: Accenture doubled its M&A budget to roughly $9 billion — nearly double the original $5 billion target. Its pick and shovel is reinvention services, the messy human work of tearing out legacy systems and plugging AI into how the world's biggest companies actually run. The strategy, in CEO Julie Sweet's words, is helping clients move “from using AI to running on AI” — and buying whatever expertise gets them there faster. AI and data-partner bookings are on track to more than double from fiscal 2025. This isn't a shopping spree for fun. It's an arms race.

You wouldn't have guessed any of this back in June. On June 18, Accenture reported a solid third quarter — revenue of $18.7 billion, up 6% in dollars, earnings per share of $3.80, up 9%, and new bookings of $19.3 billion — then promptly cut its full-year outlook, citing the impact of the Iran conflict and a roughly $100 million hit to consulting revenue. Shares tumbled about 17% to a nine-year low. It was, by any measure, a brutal day.

Since then, the comeback has been quiet and steady. Shares have climbed more than 50% off their June lows, and this week the analysts came along for the ride: Citigroup raised its target from $135 to $190, Wolfe Research from $165 to $215, and TD Cowen from $151 to $173, while UBS reiterated its Buy rating. The Street is starting to price in a thesis that would have sounded crazy in June: the biggest deployer of enterprise AI on Earth might be exactly where you want to be.

It's not just SAP deals, either. Accenture spent the quarter bulking up cybersecurity, taking a majority stake in Dragos and adding runZero and NetRise — a more than $4 billion push on top of a cyber business already generating $10 billion in annual revenue. It also boosted its fiscal 2026 share-repurchase program to $7.5 billion, with planned shareholder returns of $11.5 billion for the year. Sweet's own line from the quarter sums up the confidence: “Demand for large-scale reinvention remains strong — 104 quarterly client bookings of $100 million or more year-to-date, up 13%.”

The bottom line: the “AI eats consulting” fear is real, and Accenture's answer is to buy its way to relevance at a pace no rival can match. Whether $9 billion is enough remains to be seen. But the firm with the most to lose is placing the biggest bet — and that's exactly the kind of conviction you want from the market leader.

Disclosure: The Signal holds no position in ACN. Positions may change. This is not financial advice.
